headline: Hennessy highlights BHP's copper exposure as a meaningful conduit for AI thematic within the Australian equity index
reasoning: While the conventional view is that Australia has very little AI thematic exposure within its equity index, Hennessy argues that looking at BHP and its copper exposure changes the picture. Copper is a key input for AI infrastructure buildout, and through this lens the Australian market may have 5-10% AI thematic exposure — still low compared to global equities but more than commonly appreciated.
quote: I suppose if you dig down a little bit and you look at the likes of BHP and its exposure to copper and these sorts of sectors, it's probably more like 5 to 10% of our market has some sort of exposure to the the AI thematic still low compared to, say, global equities.

headline: Zenith estimates ~15% of a typical balanced Australian portfolio is now exposed to the AI thematic across equities, rates, infrastructure and credit
reasoning: Hennessy walked through a cross-asset exercise estimating AI thematic exposure: Australian equities ~5-10% (copper via BHP a key driver), global equities ~35%, global rates ~10% (data centres), infrastructure 10-20% (power grid/AI power), and investment-grade credit ~3% (hyperscaler issuance). In aggregate, Zenith estimates ~15% of a balanced Australian portfolio is AI-exposed. For context, banks represent only 8-10% of a typical Australian balanced portfolio, making the AI thematic double the weight of banks — a dramatic shift from 3-4 years ago.
quote: What we did an exercise where we went through each of the asset classes and said well how much of that is exposed to the AI theme? Let's start maybe with Australia. I mean, the the belief is that Australia has very little, uh, AI thematic within its index. But I suppose if you dig down a little bit and you look at the likes of BHP and its exposure to copper and these sorts of sectors, it's probably more like 5 to 10% of our market has some sort of exposure to the the AI thematic still low compared to, say, global equities. Global equities would be more like 35% we estimate with the the AI thematic as part of it. If you look at rates, global rates, probably 10% of global rates are in data centers... you put all those asset classes together and you've got something like we think around about 15% of your portfolio exposed to the AI thematic.
episode_title: Why Damien sees higher for longer T-bills

headline: Hennessy sees selective opportunity in Australian resources, particularly copper, but remains cautious on iron ore due to weak Chinese demand
reasoning: Hennessy acknowledges that copper has benefited miners like BHP and Rio and sees reasons that could continue. However, he draws a distinction with iron ore, citing weak demand out of China. He emphasises selectivity is required when investing in Australian equities, particularly within the mining sector. The broader resource recovery or boom is hard to sustain given China's economic struggles.
quote: Different story with iron ore is to say particularly demand out of China. I think you have to be just selective, though. I think you're careful about where you're exposed in Australian equities. You know, outside the mining sector earnings. You know the earnings season has been very mixed. Perhaps growth of you know sort of mid to high single digits is probably about as good as we can see.

headline: Hennessy expects Warsh at Jackson Hole to focus on inflation concerns and the emerging productivity story as a disinflationary force
reasoning: Hennessy expects Fed Chair Kevin Warsh to use the Jackson Hole Symposium to address inflation concerns while also discussing productivity gains that could keep inflation lower than otherwise expected. Warsh has been very quiet and selective with his comments so far, so more clarity on his thinking around interest rates — particularly the long end — is anticipated. However, Hennessy reiterates that Warsh has limited ability to influence the long end of the bond market.
quote: I think we have to hear more from him because he's been very quiet and selective with his comments so far. So I think we'll hear more about his task force forces. But I think particularly we'll hear a little bit more about the thinking around interest rates and perhaps on the long end of the market. Now, Warsh can do very little to impact the long end of the US bond market. And as we've seen, I think US Treasury can do little on that front as well. So I think what we can expect from Warsh at the end of this week is more around, look where we're concerned about inflation. But I think he's also going to talk about the productivity story and that there's signs that productivity is emerging. And that will tend to keep the level of inflation lower than what it would otherwise be.

headline: Damien Hennessy sees US 30-year yields staying elevated, with Treasury and Fed having limited ability to bring long-end rates down
reasoning: The US 30-year bond remains well above 5%, and Hennessy believes neither the US Treasury nor the Fed Chair Kevin Warsh can do much to bring long-end rates lower. The US is now running $40 trillion in debt with over $1 trillion in annual interest costs, representing 19% of the budget deficit. Mortgage rates at ~6.8% are already impacting the real economy. While there is political pressure ahead of midterm elections to lower rates, Hennessy thinks it is unlikely the Fed will cut at the short end, with the bias arguably still toward tightening.
quote: The US 30 year is still well above 5%. So that's a problem. Um, it's a difficult one I can. I mean, the US is running up a significant level of debt now. You know, we saw the 40 trillion number mentioned the other day. Uh, the interest costs on that are upwards of 1 trillion. So 19% of the budget deficit is actually spent just on interest expenses only... So I would think that Trump is trying to get Treasury to sort of get the level of interest rates down... It seems unlikely that that's going to happen at the short end. You know the fed funds rate uh, Kevin Warsh is even though he's he's held back from tightening I think the bias is still there to to lift rates.
